>> >> I am slightly confused by some results I'm getting when
>> >> analysing some antelope data using Distance. For a
>> >> particular data set, the model with the lowest AIC value
>> >> does not necessarily have the lowest %CV. This is despite
>> >> each model being based on the same number of data points.
>> >>
>> >> I realise that in general people focus on achieving lower
>> >> %CVs but I assume this is because they are comparing
>> >> results with different numbers of sample points. Should I
>> >> be doing the same when choosing which model is best for
>> >> this particular data set, even if the AIC results suggests
>> >> I should use a different model?
> >
> >Thomasina, a small cv is only good if the model gives approximately
> >unbiased estimates. An exponential model for example will often give a
> >small cv but a poor AIC. The latter indicates that it fits the data
> >poorly, so its estimate may prove to be very unreliable, and its higher
> >precision highly misleading. This issue is covered in our distance
> >sampling book, which can be accessed on the web:
> >
> >http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancebook/
> >
> >Only go for a model with small cv if you are satisfied it provides a good
> >fit to your data - and use AIC, goodness-of-fit and histograms to make
> >this assessment. Don't rely on a single cookbook rule.
> >
